# Nightly run failed on a cart nobody can get back

## Problem Description

Tuesday's nightly failed in `tests/pricing.test.js` with `AssertionError:
expected 9 to be less than 9`. The reporter printed those two numbers and
nothing else - not the cart, not the customer tier, not the line items.

Nobody has seen it since. The suite has run green roughly forty times, on
laptops and on CI, and re-running the failed job went green immediately. We
cannot put the suite back into the state that produced that number, so we
cannot say whether the bug is still there or whether the price ranges someone
tightened in the factory last month happen to hide it.

Three suites build their data from `tests/factories/cart.js`, so whatever we do
here applies to the rest of them too.

## Output Specification

1. When a run fails, the report must carry whatever a developer needs to re-run
   the suite over exactly the data that failed, and re-running that way must
   produce that data again.
2. Two runs of the unchanged suite must build the same data - on a laptop and
   on CI, in any order.
3. The data must stay generated and varied. Freezing the fields to constant
   values is not an acceptable way to get repeatability; long names, odd
   addresses and awkward prices are the reason the factory exists.
4. Write down, in one or two lines somewhere a developer will find them, how to
   reproduce a failed run from what the report prints.
5. Do not change `src/pricing.js`, and leave both existing tests asserting what
   they assert today. `npm test` must stay green.
evals.expected_output:
1. When a run fails, the report must carry whatever a developer needs to re-run
   the suite over exactly the data that failed, and re-running that way must
   produce that data again.
2. Two runs of the unchanged suite must build the same data - on a laptop and
   on CI, in any order.
3. The data must stay generated and varied. Freezing the fields to constant
   values is not an acceptable way to get repeatability; long names, odd
   addresses and awkward prices are the reason the factory exists.
4. Write down, in one or two lines somewhere a developer will find them, how to
   reproduce a failed run from what the report prints.
5. Do not change `src/pricing.js`, and leave both existing tests asserting what
   they assert today. `npm test` must stay green.
assertions: `npm test` exits clean with both existing tests running and asserting what they assert today. A suite that no longer collects, or that had an assertion weakened to accommodate the change, scores zero.

The random stream is pinned by an explicit seed call, and it is applied per test - a `beforeEach`, a setup file registered as a per-test hook, or an explicit seed at the top of each test - so a given test builds the same data whether the file runs whole, filtered to one test, or with a new test inserted above it. A single seed call evaluated once at module load (top of the factory or top of the spec) scores at most half: the whole file is reproducible but any individual test is not, which is the exact shape that makes a CI failure unreproducible from a filtered local run. No seed call anywhere scores zero.

The value used is visible in the run output (printed by the setup, attached to the reporter, or written to an artifact) and can be supplied back on the next run - an env var or CLI argument with a sensible default. A hardcoded constant that is never surfaced scores at most half: it is reproducible but the report still tells the developer nothing, and every run exercises the same handful of records forever. Nothing surfaced and no override scores zero.

MUST NOT leave any generating call outside the seeded window - factory values computed at module import time before the hook runs, a second generator instance created elsewhere, `Math.random`/`Date.now` used for ids or quantities, or a seed call placed after the data is built. Any such path scores zero for this item; it is the anti-pattern this scenario exists to catch, because it produces a suite that looks seeded and still drifts.

The factory still produces varied values from the data generator for names, emails, SKUs, prices and quantities. Replacing any of those with a constant literal, a fixed array cycled through, or an incrementing counter to buy determinism scores zero - the requirement was reproducible generation, not the removal of generation.

New or edited assertions compare against values derived from the same generated input (as the existing tests do), not against literal names, prices or ids captured from a seeded run. Any pasted literal that came out of a generated run scores zero here, since it re-breaks the moment the seed or the library version changes.

A README line, a comment in the setup file, or a contributing note states how to take the value from a failed report and re-run against it, with the concrete command. Only mentioning it in the chat response scores zero; the fix has to survive the conversation.
MUST NOT edit `src/pricing.js` or add dependencies to package.json. Both were declared out of scope; either scores zero here.

# Nothing in the suite ever inserts a second account

## Problem Description

`tests/factories.py` hands back the same person every time: John Doe,
`johndoe`, `john.doe@example.com`. The repository has unique constraints on the
username and the email, so the second `repo.add(make_account())` in any test
raises, and over time everybody just stopped writing tests that add more than
one account.

That has cost us. The signup endpoint returned a 500 instead of a 409 for a
duplicate email for eight months and no test noticed, because no test ever got
as far as a duplicate. The search test cannot tell records apart - every record
matches every query. The load-test seeder that builds 5,000 accounts had to
grow its own counter to get past the constraints, so its data looks nothing like
the data the tests use.

## Output Specification

1. `make_account()` must return a distinct, realistic account on every call: a
   person's name, a username and an email address that no other generated
   account in the same run shares.
2. Prove it: a test that builds 5,000 accounts in one run and finds no
   collision on either constrained field.
3. A suite must be able to add many accounts to one repository without tripping
   the unique constraints by accident.
4. Add a test that deliberately adds a duplicate email and expects the conflict
   the repository raises - that path must be exercised on purpose.
5. One test's generation must not affect another test's - the suite must pass
   whether it runs whole or a single test runs alone, and a failing run must be
   repeatable.
6. Do not edit `repository.py`. `pytest` must stay green.
evals.expected_output:
1. `make_account()` must return a distinct, realistic account on every call: a
   person's name, a username and an email address that no other generated
   account in the same run shares.
2. Prove it: a test that builds 5,000 accounts in one run and finds no
   collision on either constrained field.
3. A suite must be able to add many accounts to one repository without tripping
   the unique constraints by accident.
4. Add a test that deliberately adds a duplicate email and expects the conflict
   the repository raises - that path must be exercised on purpose.
5. One test's generation must not affect another test's - the suite must pass
   whether it runs whole or a single test runs alone, and a failing run must be
   repeatable.
6. Do not edit `repository.py`. `pytest` must stay green.
assertions: `pytest` exits clean including the new batch test. A failing or erroring run scores zero.

Username and email are produced through a mechanism that cannot repeat within a run - the library's uniqueness facility, or an explicit guarantee such as a rejection loop against a seen-set. Full credit requires both constrained fields covered. Calling the plain providers and relying on the value space to be large enough scores at most half: at 5,000 records the collision is close to certain, and this is the specific failure the batch test exists to catch. Leaving either field constant scores zero.

A test generates the full batch in one run and asserts the number of distinct usernames and distinct emails equals the batch size (or adds all of them to a repository without a conflict being raised). A test that samples ten records scores at most half - it cannot detect what is being claimed.

Names, usernames and emails are drawn from the person and internet providers rather than composed from indexes. A factory returning `user_1@example.com` / `Test User 1` style values scores zero: uniqueness was one of two requirements and realism was the other, and index-composed data never exercises the apostrophe, long-name or non-ASCII paths.

A test adds an account, then adds a second account carrying the same email (via an override), and asserts the repository's specific duplicate-email error is raised. Asserting only that 'an exception' is raised scores at most half - the eight-month bug was a wrong error, not a missing one. No such test scores zero.

Whatever tracks already-issued values is reset per test - the library's uniqueness reset call in a fixture, or a per-test generator instance. A module-level uniqueness pool shared by the whole session scores at most half: it survives this suite and starts exhausting or cross-contaminating as soon as a second batch test is added.

MUST NOT leave the generation unseeded. The random stream is fixed by an explicit seed so a collision or a failing record can be produced again on demand; an unseeded batch test that fails once in fifty runs is exactly the unreproducible failure this repo already suffers from. No seeding scores zero.
MUST NOT edit `repository.py`, and the two existing tests keep passing unmodified. Either scores zero here.

# Inventory tests can't be run one at a time

## Problem Description

Two things keep biting us in `tests/inventory.test.js`.

Running a single test fails. `npm test -- -t "drops out of the in-stock list"`
goes red, because that test only passes when the reservation test ran first and
emptied an item. Whole-file runs are green, so nobody noticed until someone
tried to debug that one test.

And last week Priya added a test at the top of the file. Her change had nothing
to do with the two tests below it, but every SKU and product name those tests
generate came out different. She was midway through chasing a bug she had
reproduced from one specific SKU, and the reproduction disappeared - the log
lines she had collected no longer matched anything the suite produced.

## Output Specification

1. Each test must work with its own data and must not depend on what another
   test did to a shared object. The suite must pass whole, and each test must
   pass when it is the only one that runs.
2. The data a given test receives must not change when an unrelated test is
   added above it, removed, or when the run is filtered to one test.
3. Two runs of the unchanged file must produce the same data, so a SKU from a
   log line still means something tomorrow.
4. The data must stay generated - names, SKUs and prices keep coming from the
   generator, not from literals typed into the tests.
5. Keep the four behaviours the file covers today. Do not edit
   `src/inventory.js`. `npm test` must stay green.
evals.expected_output:
1. Each test must work with its own data and must not depend on what another
   test did to a shared object. The suite must pass whole, and each test must
   pass when it is the only one that runs.
2. The data a given test receives must not change when an unrelated test is
   added above it, removed, or when the run is filtered to one test.
3. Two runs of the unchanged file must produce the same data, so a SKU from a
   log line still means something tomorrow.
4. The data must stay generated - names, SKUs and prices keep coming from the
   generator, not from literals typed into the tests.
5. Keep the four behaviours the file covers today. Do not edit
   `src/inventory.js`. `npm test` must stay green.
assertions: `npm test` is green, and each of the four tests also passes when it is the only one selected. Any test that still needs a predecessor to have run scores zero here - that is the first reported symptom.

An explicit seed call runs at the start of every test - a `beforeEach`, a per-test hook registered in setup, or an explicit call inside each test - so a given test's draws begin from the same point no matter what ran before it. Moving generation into a per-test hook while the single module-load seed call stays scores zero for this item, even though the suite then passes in any order: the values a test receives still depend on its position in the file, which is the second symptom the task describes. No seeding at all also scores zero.

The catalogue and the inventory instance are built per test rather than once at module load. A module-level object that tests mutate scores zero. Rebuilding per test but still sharing one array reference that a test mutates scores at most half.

MUST NOT stabilise the file by writing literal SKUs, product names or prices into the tests, or by freezing the factory to constants. Any such literal scores zero: repeatability was required alongside generated data, not instead of it.

MUST NOT resolve the isolation problem by pinning execution order - disabling shuffling, forcing sequential or single-threaded execution, merging the dependent tests into one, or documenting that they must run in order. Any of those scores zero; the requirement was that each test stands alone.

All four behaviours - full reservation, the in-stock list after depletion, a new arrival joining the list, and over-reservation throwing - are still asserted, with the depletion case now creating its own depleted item. Dropping or weakening one scores zero.

`tests/factories/item.js` still generates each field from the generator, and any change to it serves per-test construction rather than removing generation. Rewriting the factory to accept a fixed data table scores zero.
MUST NOT edit `src/inventory.js` or add dependencies. Either scores zero here.

# Half of contact.js has no tests because our fixtures can't reach it

## Problem Description

`tests/factories/contact.js` fills every field with filler text: the name is two
random words, the postcode is five random letters and digits, the date of birth
is the same hardcoded string for every contact, and the account number is a
random alphanumeric blob.

The consequence is that `isDeliverable`, `isAdult` and `maskAccountNumber` are
untested. `isDeliverable` wants a postcode that looks like a postcode and our
factory cannot produce one, so the first attempt at a test wrote its own
literal contact inline, which then drifted from the factory and was deleted.
`maskAccountNumber` shipped a bug last quarter (it returned `****` for anything
with fewer than five digits, and half of our fixtures have zero digits, so
nothing caught it).

Separately, in April a customer whose display name contained
`<script>alert(1)</script>` had it rendered raw in an internal back-office tool.
`escapeName` was written for that and never covered.

## Output Specification

1. Rework `tests/factories/contact.js` so each field is produced by a source
   that matches what the field holds: a person's name, an address whose street,
   city and postcode satisfy the app's address rule, a dialable phone number, a
   date of birth that puts the contact in adult range, and an account number in
   a payment-like shape.
2. Add tests for `isDeliverable`, `isAdult` and `maskAccountNumber` that run
   against factory output rather than literals written into each test.
3. Cover the April incident: `escapeName` must be exercised with that exact
   input.
4. Two runs of the suite must produce the same data.
5. Do not edit `src/contact.js`; the two existing tests keep asserting what they
   assert. `npm test` must stay green.
evals.expected_output:
1. Rework `tests/factories/contact.js` so each field is produced by a source
   that matches what the field holds: a person's name, an address whose street,
   city and postcode satisfy the app's address rule, a dialable phone number, a
   date of birth that puts the contact in adult range, and an account number in
   a payment-like shape.
2. Add tests for `isDeliverable`, `isAdult` and `maskAccountNumber` that run
   against factory output rather than literals written into each test.
3. Cover the April incident: `escapeName` must be exercised with that exact
   input.
4. Two runs of the suite must produce the same data.
5. Do not edit `src/contact.js`; the two existing tests keep asserting what they
   assert. `npm test` must stay green.
assertions: `npm test` exits clean with both existing tests plus the new ones. Any failure or collection error scores zero.

Name from the person provider, email from the internet provider, street / city / postcode from the location provider, phone from the phone provider, account number from the finance provider. Full credit requires all of them; hand-assembling any of these from random digits, characters or filler words scores at most half overall for this item, and leaving two or more fields on filler text scores zero. The point is that the values are drawn from real-world datasets - that is what surfaces long names, accented characters and hyphenated place names.

The date comes from the generator's date provider constrained to an age or date window that keeps the contact an adult (a birthdate helper with min/max age, or an explicit date range). A hardcoded date scores zero - that is the current defect. An unconstrained random date, which can produce a contact born last week or in 1804, scores at most half: it makes `isAdult` tests flip between runs.

`isDeliverable`, `isAdult` and `maskAccountNumber` each get a test whose input comes from `makeContact` (with overrides where a specific case is needed), not a literal contact object written inline. Full credit needs all three covered. Tests that rebuild a contact literal inline score at most half - that is the drift the team already deleted once.

MUST NOT ask the data generator to produce the adversarial input. The `escapeName` test passes the exact `<script>alert(1)</script>` string as a literal (or an override carrying it). Generating a 'random malicious' / 'special character' / 'random symbols' value for that case scores zero: the generator produces plausible real-world values, so a script tag will never occur by chance and the test would be permanently vacuous.

The generator's random stream is fixed by an explicit seed so a failing run can be repeated. No seed anywhere scores zero. A seed set once at module load scores at most half, since a filtered run then produces different data than the full run.
Repeated `makeContact()` calls still produce distinct ids, whether via the existing counter or a generated identifier. Replacing the counter with a value that repeats within a run scores zero.
MUST NOT edit `src/contact.js` or add dependencies. Either scores zero here; the production behaviour was explicitly not in question.

# Nothing our factory generates gets past the contact API

## Problem Description

`registerContact` requires E.164 (`+` then digits, no separators) because that
is the form the SMS provider accepts. Our factory hands out numbers like
`(551) 526-4392`, so the staging seeder dies on the first contact and the
contact path has no coverage against generated data at all - the only phone
tests we have use three numbers somebody typed by hand.

A branch tried stripping the punctuation, which produced `5515264392` and was
rejected too, then prefixing `+1` to the stripped digits. That got the US seed
run through. We also seed a German region, and those contacts went in as `+1`
numbers with German digits behind them, which the SMS provider accepted and then
failed to deliver.

`isE164` is not up for discussion - it matches what the provider documents.

## Output Specification

1. Generated contacts must satisfy the contact API as they come out of the
   factory. Prove it with a test that builds 500 contacts and registers every
   one of them without a rejection.
2. We seed two regions, US and Germany. Both must produce numbers the API
   accepts, and a German contact's number must be a German number - not a
   German-looking string behind a US country code.
3. Numbers must stay varied. One constant number for every contact is not
   acceptable; the staging data is used to eyeball the contact list.
4. `scripts/seed-staging.js` must get its contacts from the same factory the
   tests use.
5. Two runs must produce the same contacts.
6. Do not edit `src/validation.js`. `npm test` must stay green.
evals.expected_output:
1. Generated contacts must satisfy the contact API as they come out of the
   factory. Prove it with a test that builds 500 contacts and registers every
   one of them without a rejection.
2. We seed two regions, US and Germany. Both must produce numbers the API
   accepts, and a German contact's number must be a German number - not a
   German-looking string behind a US country code.
3. Numbers must stay varied. One constant number for every contact is not
   acceptable; the staging data is used to eyeball the contact list.
4. `scripts/seed-staging.js` must get its contacts from the same factory the
   tests use.
5. Two runs must produce the same contacts.
6. Do not edit `src/validation.js`. `npm test` must stay green.
assertions: `npm test` exits clean with the three existing tests plus the new batch test. A failing or uncollectable suite scores zero.

The phone value comes out of the phone provider already in E.164 - the provider's international style option, or an explicit format template passed to it - for each region, rather than being repaired afterwards. Assembling the number from a hardcoded country-code string plus generated digits scores at most half. Leaving the default call and transforming the result scores at most half, and scores zero if the country code applied is a constant shared across regions, which is the delivery failure described in the task.

MUST NOT make the batch pass by validating inside the factory and retrying, filtering rejected contacts out of the batch, or wrapping registration in a try/catch that swallows the rejection. Any of those scores zero: it converts a generator that produces unusable data into a green test, and the seeding script would still be discarding most of what it makes.

A test builds 500 contacts and registers every one of them, with both regions represented, asserting no rejection. A test of a handful of contacts scores at most half, and one that checks only the default region scores at most half - the German path is where the previous fix failed.

German contacts are generated from the German locale's phone data (a locale-specific generator instance or an equivalent), so the digits and the country code agree. A German contact whose digits come from the default locale scores zero here, even if the string satisfies `isE164`.

Contacts differ from each other; the value is still generated per contact. A single constant number, or a counter-derived sequence, scores zero - the staging contact list has to be readable as distinct people.

MUST NOT leave the batch unseeded. The stream is fixed by an explicit seed so a rejected contact can be produced again; an unseeded 500-record test that fails once a fortnight is unchaseable. No seeding scores zero.

`scripts/seed-staging.js` still gets contacts from the shared factory and therefore inherits the fix. Duplicating a corrected phone helper inside the script, or leaving the script on the old path, scores zero.

MUST NOT edit `src/validation.js` - not the regex, not the error, not the register function. The rule mirrors the provider's documented requirement and was declared out of scope; any edit scores zero.

# Every order in our fixtures belongs to a customer who doesn't exist

## Problem Description

`makeOrder()` generates its own `userId`, so no generated order has ever
belonged to a generated user. `customerOrderReport` skips orders whose user it
cannot find, which means every report row our tests produce says zero orders and
zero revenue - and the tests pass, because they only check the number of rows
and the name on each row.

That caught up with us. A change to the reporting query stopped joining orders
at all. Production reports went out with every customer at $0. The suite was
green through the whole thing.

Two more things make the factory unusable for the ageing report we are about to
write: `totalCents` is generated independently of the line items, so it never
matches the sum of them, and `shippedAt` is generated in the same window as
`placedAt`, so roughly half of our orders ship before they are placed.

## Output Specification

1. A generated order must belong to a real user: the factory either creates the
   user alongside the order or accepts one, and the order's `userId` is that
   user's id. Callers must still be able to pass their own user.
2. Generated records must be internally consistent: an order's total equals the
   sum of its line items, and an order that has shipped shipped after it was
   placed.
3. Add a test that proves the linkage over a batch - every order in a generated
   set points at a user in that set.
4. The report tests must be able to fail: after the change, a report built from
   generated users and orders must show real counts and totals, and the suite
   must go red if the join is dropped again.
5. Two runs must produce the same data.
6. Do not edit `src/report.js`. `npm test` must stay green.
evals.expected_output:
1. A generated order must belong to a real user: the factory either creates the
   user alongside the order or accepts one, and the order's `userId` is that
   user's id. Callers must still be able to pass their own user.
2. Generated records must be internally consistent: an order's total equals the
   sum of its line items, and an order that has shipped shipped after it was
   placed.
3. Add a test that proves the linkage over a batch - every order in a generated
   set points at a user in that set.
4. The report tests must be able to fail: after the change, a report built from
   generated users and orders must show real counts and totals, and the suite
   must go red if the join is dropped again.
5. Two runs must produce the same data.
6. Do not edit `src/report.js`. `npm test` must stay green.
assertions: `npm test` exits clean with the existing tests plus the new ones. A failing or uncollectable suite scores zero.

Calling the order factory with no arguments yields an order attached to a user the caller can reach - the factory creates the user and exposes it (returns the pair, or takes and defaults a user parameter), and an explicit user passed by the caller is used instead of a fresh one. Fixing only the call sites while `makeOrder()` still invents a `userId` scores zero: the next caller gets an orphan. A factory that creates a user internally but gives the caller no way to obtain it scores at most half - the report cannot be built from it.

An order's total is derived from its own line items rather than generated separately, and `shippedAt` is generated after `placedAt` (or omitted for unshipped orders) using a date range anchored on the placed date. Fixing one of the two scores at most half; fixing neither scores zero. Both are cases of one generated field having to respect another, which independent draws cannot do.

A test builds several users and orders and asserts every order's `userId` resolves to a user in the set. Asserting it for a single hand-wired pair scores at most half - the current bug is exactly that a single pair looks right when wired by hand.

At least one report assertion checks a non-zero count and a total derived from the generated orders, so dropping the join turns the suite red. If every report assertion would still pass when `customerOrderReport` skips every order, this scores zero - that is the regression the work exists to catch.

The generator's stream is fixed by an explicit seed applied per test rather than once at module load, so an individual failing test can be re-run over the same graph. No seeding scores zero; a single module-load seed scores at most half.

MUST NOT assert against literal ids, names or totals captured from a generated run. Expectations are computed from the same generated records. Any pasted literal scores zero: it binds the suite to one version's random sequence and re-breaks on the next dependency bump.
MUST NOT edit `src/report.js` or add dependencies. The reporting behaviour, including skipping orphan orders, was explicitly not in question; either scores zero here.

# Profile suite can't be pointed at the German or Japanese market

## Problem Description

We ship the profile page in three markets next month: US, Germany and Japan.
The profile suite only knows about the US one. Everything it builds is a US
person at a US address, and two of the assertions have quietly baked that in.

The first attempt at Japanese coverage failed immediately. `initials` splits the
full name on a space, and the Japanese names we tried have no space in them, so
the assertion that a profile has at least two initials failed. Somebody
"fixed" it by leaving the Japanese profiles on US names, which passes and tests
nothing.

The postcode assertion has the same problem in the other direction: German
postcodes are five digits with no extension, Japanese ones carry a hyphen in a
different place, and the current pattern only describes the US format.

## Output Specification

1. The profile factory must be able to build a profile for the US, German and
   Japanese markets, where the name, city, street, postcode and phone number
   are that market's real formats rather than US values with a market label
   attached.
2. Assertions that hold in only one market must not be applied to the others.
   The initials rule and the postcode pattern are the two known cases; check
   for others while you are in there.
3. Each market's postcode and phone assertions must describe that market's
   actual format, and the suite must fail if a market silently comes back with
   US-shaped data.
4. Two runs of the suite must produce the same data.
5. The three existing US tests must keep passing and keep asserting what they
   assert today. Do not edit `src/profile.js`. `npm test` must stay green.
evals.expected_output:
1. The profile factory must be able to build a profile for the US, German and
   Japanese markets, where the name, city, street, postcode and phone number
   are that market's real formats rather than US values with a market label
   attached.
2. Assertions that hold in only one market must not be applied to the others.
   The initials rule and the postcode pattern are the two known cases; check
   for others while you are in there.
3. Each market's postcode and phone assertions must describe that market's
   actual format, and the suite must fail if a market silently comes back with
   US-shaped data.
4. Two runs of the suite must produce the same data.
5. The three existing US tests must keep passing and keep asserting what they
   assert today. Do not edit `src/profile.js`. `npm test` must stay green.
assertions: `npm test` exits clean, the three existing tests still assert what they assert today. Deleting, skipping or loosening one of them to make room for the new markets scores zero.

German and Japanese profiles are produced by pointing the generator at those locales - the locale-specific generator exports, or a generator instance constructed with the locale's dataset - so names, cities, streets, postcodes and phone numbers all come from that market's data. Hand-written arrays of names or cities, transliterating US values, or building a locale-shaped postcode from random digits scores zero, no matter how many markets it covers. Pointing only the name field at the locale while the address stays on the default generator scores at most half.

MUST NOT keep the space-separated-name assumption (splitting on a space, expecting at least two initials) in a market whose names have no space, and MUST NOT keep the Japanese or German profiles on US names to preserve it. Either scores zero here. Also zero if the fix is to make the shared assertion vacuous for everyone - the US behaviour still has to be checked.

Postcode and phone expectations are per market and describe that market's actual shape. A single permissive pattern that all three markets satisfy scores at most half: it passes, and it no longer detects a market coming back with the wrong country's data - which is exactly the regression this work exists to prevent.

At least one assertion per market would fail if that market silently produced default US data - a postcode pattern that US values cannot satisfy, a check that the city is drawn from that locale, or equivalent. A suite where every new test would still pass on US values scores zero: locale coverage in these libraries is uneven and a missing dataset falls back quietly.

The market-independent behaviour (address formatting, id presence) is exercised through one table or loop over the markets rather than three duplicated blocks. Three near-identical copies of the file score at most half.

Every generator instance in play, including the per-market ones, has its random stream fixed by an explicit seed.
